var vs let vs const?

| var | let | const
Scope | Function | Block | Block
Hoisting | Hoisted and initialized to undefined | Hoisted but in the TDZ (ReferenceError) | TDZ
Re-declare | Yes | No | No
Reassign | Yes | Yes | No (the object can still be mutated)
What is hoisting?

Declarations are moved to the top of their scope during compilation. Function declarations are fully hoisted, so you can call them before they're defined. var is hoisted as undefined. let, const and class are hoisted but sit in the Temporal Dead Zone until their declaration runs. Function expressions and arrow functions follow the rules of the variable they're assigned to.

How does this work? Arrow vs normal functions?

this depends on how a function is called: as a method it's the object · as a plain call it's undefined in strict mode (or window otherwise) · with new it's the new instance · with call/apply/bind it's whatever you pass · in event handlers it's the element. Arrow functions have no this of their own; they inherit it from the enclosing scope (lexical this). They also have no arguments and can't be used with new.
call vs apply vs bind?
fn.call(obj, a, b) invokes now with arguments listed out · fn.apply(obj, [a, b]) invokes now with an array · fn.bind(obj, a) returns a new function with this fixed, to call later.
== vs ===? Truthy/falsy?

== converts types before comparing ('5' == 5 is true, null == undefined is true). === is strict: no conversion. Always use ===. The falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including [] and {}.
null vs undefined?

undefined: declared but not assigned, a missing property, or no return value. null: explicitly set to "no value". typeof null === 'object' is a historical bug. Use ?? (nullish coalescing) and ?. (optional chaining).

map vs forEach vs filter vs reduce?

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
nums.map(n => n * 2);              // [2,4,6,8]  new array
nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);     // [2,4]
nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0); // 10
nums.forEach(n => console.log(n)); // returns undefined (side-effects only)
Shallow copy vs deep copy?

A shallow copy ({...obj}, Object.assign, [...arr]) copies only the top level, so nested objects are still shared. A deep copy uses structuredClone(obj) (modern) or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), which loses Dates, functions and undefined, and fails on cycles.
Event bubbling, capturing and delegation?

Events travel in three phases: capture (window down to the target), target, then bubble (back up). addEventListener(type, fn, true) listens in the capture phase. stopPropagation() stops the travel and preventDefault() cancels the default action. Delegation: put one listener on a parent and check e.target, which is efficient and also works for elements added later.
What is currying? Pure functions? Higher-order functions?
Currying: f(a,b,c) → f(a)(b)(c). A pure function returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects. A higher-order function takes or returns functions (map, filter, debounce).
localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?

localStorage | sessionStorage | Cookie
About 5–10 MB, kept until cleared | Lasts only as long as the tab | About 4 KB, has an expiry
Readable by JS (XSS risk) | Readable by JS | Sent with every request; can be HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite
What is TypeScript and why use it (Angular)?

A typed superset of JS that compiles to JS. It gives static types, interfaces, generics, enums, access modifiers and decorators. Errors are caught at compile time, and IDE support and refactoring are better. Why can a Java long ID arrive wrong in the browser? How do you fix it?

JSON numbers are parsed into IEEE-754 doubles, which are exact only up to 2⁵³−1. JSON.parse('{"id":9007199254740993}').id gives 9007199254740992, with no error. Snowflake-style IDs and many database keys exceed this limit. The fix is on the server: send such IDs as strings, for example with @JsonSerialize(using = ToStringSerializer.class) or a global Jackson module. Treat them as opaque strings in TypeScript. BigInt is not a solution by itself, because JSON.parse has already lost the digits and JSON.stringify throws on BigInt.
for...in vs for...of vs forEach vs a classic for?

| Iterates | break | await inside works?
for | Whatever you code | Yes | Yes
for...of | Values of any iterable | Yes | Yes
for...in | Enumerable string keys, inherited too | Yes | Yes
forEach | Array items, skipping holes | No; only a throw exits | No; the promises are ignored
Do not use for...in on arrays. Keys are strings and it may include extra properties. Use arr.some or for...of if you need to stop early.
slice vs splice?

slice(start, end) copies a range and leaves the original unchanged. splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) changes the original in place and returns the removed items. The modern non-mutating version of splice is toSpliced. With Angular OnPush, you need the non-mutating forms, because a new reference is what triggers an update.
How is a class different from a constructor function?

- A class must be called with new.
- Class bodies are always strict.
- Methods are non-enumerable and have no prototype, so they cannot be used with new.
- Classes sit in the TDZ until declared.
- In a derived class, this does not exist until super() returns, because the base constructor allocates the object. That is also why extending Array or Error works with classes.
- Only classes offer #private, fields, and static blocks.
#private vs TypeScript private vs closure privacy?

TypeScript private exists only at compile time, so at run time the field is an ordinary property. #field is enforced by the engine, and access from outside is a SyntaxError. It also cannot be seen by Object.keys or Proxy: a method using #x called on a Proxy wrapper throws a TypeError. Closure variables are private too, but they cost one function per instance, and other instances cannot reach them. #x can be read on any instance of the same class, like Java's private.
How do you make an object iterable?

Objects are not iterable by default, so for (const x of {}) throws a TypeError. Add a [Symbol.iterator] method that returns an object with next(), usually by writing it as a generator: *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* Object.entries(this); }. Iterables are consumed by for...of, spread, array destructuring, Array.from, new Map, new Set and Promise.all. A generator object is its own iterator, so it can only be consumed once.
target vs currentTarget; stopPropagation vs stopImmediatePropagation vs preventDefault?

target is where the event began and currentTarget is where the listener sits, which is exactly the difference that matters in delegation. stopPropagation stops the event from reaching further elements, stopImmediatePropagation also blocks later listeners on the same element, and preventDefault cancels the browser's action and does not affect propagation. Avoid stopPropagation in app code, since it silently breaks delegated handlers and analytics higher up the tree.
What does a passive event listener do?

For touchstart and wheel, the browser must normally wait for your handler in case it calls preventDefault to stop the scroll. { passive: true } tells it you will not, so the compositor can scroll at once, without waiting for the main thread. Browsers treat these listeners as passive by default on window, document and body. Calling preventDefault in a passive listener is ignored and logs a console warning.
Where should a JWT or session token live in the browser?

Each option has a trade-off.
- localStorage: simple, but any XSS can read and steal the token.
- HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie: script cannot read it, which limits the damage of XSS, but the browser sends it automatically, so you need CSRF protection (SameSite and a CSRF token).
- Short-lived access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie: a common compromise; a page reload silently gets a new access token.
No storage choice saves you from XSS completely, since a script on your page can make authenticated calls. So also apply a Content Security Policy and output encoding.
How do you keep tabs in sync?

Writing to localStorage fires a storage event in the other tabs of the same origin, not in the tab that wrote. A cleaner API is BroadcastChannel: const c = new BroadcastChannel('auth'); c.postMessage('logout'); c.onmessage = ..., which sends structured data and also works in workers. Use cases are logging out everywhere and keeping a cart in sync.
When would you use IndexedDB instead of localStorage?

Use IndexedDB when the data is large, needs indexes or range queries, consists of objects or Blobs, or must be read from a worker or service worker. Examples are offline PWA data and client-side caches of many records. localStorage is synchronous, so each read blocks the main thread, and it is limited to a few MB of strings, which suits small preferences. The IndexedDB API is event-based and verbose, so wrappers such as idb or Dexie are common.
What is XSS in plain JavaScript, and which APIs are dangerous?

XSS happens when untrusted text is treated as code. Dangerous sinks are innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, new Function, setTimeout with a string, and href set to a javascript: URL. Safe alternatives are textContent, setAttribute for known attributes, and createElement. Where HTML is required, sanitise with a library such as DOMPurify. Add a Content Security Policy as a second layer. Angular sanitises template bindings automatically, unless you bypass it with DomSanitizer.
Number vs BigInt: what are the rules?

Number is a 64-bit double, safe up to ±(2⁵³−1) as integers. BigInt is arbitrary precision, written 10n or BigInt('10'). You cannot mix them in arithmetic: 1n + 1 is a TypeError. Comparison does work (1n == 1 is true, 1n === 1 is false). Math functions do not accept BigInt, division truncates (7n / 2n is 3n), and JSON.stringify throws. It is also slower, so use it only when you need the range.
How does JS compare object contents, and what is the cost of each way?

There is no built-in deep comparison. JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b) depends on key order and loses undefined, Dates and so on. A recursive compare (see the deepEqual question) or a library such as lodash.isEqual is reliable. For frameworks, the usual approach is immutable updates, so that one reference check, a === b, can stand in for a deep comparison at O(1). That is the thinking behind OnPush and NgRx.
TypeScript: any vs unknown vs never; interface vs type?

any turns off checking. unknown accepts anything, but you must narrow it before use, so it is the safe choice for external data. never is the type with no values: the return type of a function that always throws, and the result of an exhaustive switch, which gives a compile error if a case is missing. interface describes object shapes, can be extended and merged across declarations. type can also name unions, tuples, mapped and conditional types. All TypeScript types are erased at compile time, so a type does not validate a JSON response at run time. For that, use a schema validator, such as Zod.
Scenario: a user types fast and results flicker with old data. Fix it in plain JS.
How do you lazy-load images or build infinite scroll without a scroll listener?

For images, use the native loading="lazy" attribute first. For custom behaviour, use IntersectionObserver: observe a sentinel element or each image, and act when entry.isIntersecting is true. It runs off the main scroll path and is batched, unlike a scroll handler that fires many times per second and often forces layout by calling getBoundingClientRect(). Use rootMargin to start loading early, and call unobserve or disconnect when done.
What is Shadow DOM and how does it differ from Angular's emulated encapsulation?

Shadow DOM is a browser-enforced separate DOM tree: outside CSS selectors cannot reach inside, and inside styles do not leak out. Angular's default ViewEncapsulation.Emulated only simulates this by adding generated attributes (like _ngcontent-abc) to elements and rewriting selectors; global styles can still affect the component. ViewEncapsulation.ShadowDom uses real Shadow DOM. To theme a shadow component from outside, use CSS custom properties (they inherit through the boundary) and ::part().
How does client-side routing work in plain JavaScript (History API)?

history.pushState(state, '', '/orders/42') changes the URL and adds a history entry without a request; your code then renders the matching view. Back and forward buttons fire a popstate event, which you handle to re-render. replaceState changes the current entry without adding one. Because the URL is real, the server must return index.html for those paths on refresh. Frameworks such as Angular's router wrap exactly this. The newer Navigation API (navigation.addEventListener('navigate', …)) is a cleaner replacement where supported.
Why does [10, 1, 2].sort() give [1, 10, 2]? How do you sort correctly?

Without a comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so "10" comes before "2". Pass a comparator: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers, a.name.localeCompare(b.name) for text (or an Intl.Collator for large lists). sort mutates the array and is stable since ES2019; use toSorted() for a copy. 💡 Sorting objects by date: (a, b) => new Date(a.at) - new Date(b.at).
What is the difference between an attribute and a property on a DOM element?

An attribute is what is written in the HTML (getAttribute('value')), always a string. A property is the live JavaScript value on the DOM object (input.value), which can be any type. Some are linked: changing id updates both. Others are not: value and checked attributes hold the initial value, while the properties hold the current one. Angular's [value] binds a property; [attr.aria-label] binds an attribute.
How do you copy text to the clipboard, and why can it fail?

Use await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text). It returns a promise and works only in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost), usually only after a user gesture such as a click, and may need permission when reading with readText(). Wrap it in try/catch and show a fallback message. The old document.execCommand('copy') is deprecated.
